noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to describe the addition polymerisation of alkenes and draw the repeat unit given the monomer, and vice versa

primer.text: Thousands of alkene molecules can be persuaded to join hands. Under pressure and a catalyst, pi bonds open and chain growth builds poly(ethene), PVC and poly(propene). This note draws the repeat unit from the monomer and reads it backwards, since deducing either partner from the other is the skill the papers keep testing.

lessons.title: Monomers into chains
lessons.opening: Give an alkene high pressure, a catalyst and time, and thousands of molecules will each open their pi bond and shake hands with the next. The result is an addition polymer: one long saturated chain whose repeat unit is the monomer with its double bond converted to a single bond.
keyPoints: Addition polymerisation opens the pi bond of each alkene monomer to build one long saturated chain.
High pressure and a catalyst supply the conditions that persuade monomers to join.
Poly(ethene) forms from ethene; poly(chloroethene) PVC forms from chloroethene; poly(propene) from propene.
No atoms are lost in addition polymerisation, so the polymer is the only product.
The repeat unit shows the monomer's atoms joined by a single bond, bracketed with a subscript n.

low.restatement: Many alkene molecules open their double bonds and link end to end; the chain grows until huge, and the only product is the polymer itself.
low.analogy: Paperclips with one open end (the pi bond) hook onto the next clip until the chain runs off the desk - every clip used, nothing thrown away.
low.examPointer: Draw repeat units with the bond sticking out through both brackets and the n subscript - missing extension bonds is the most common drawing deduction.

medium.restatement: Atom economy is 100 percent because every monomer atom is conserved into the chain - the pi pair redistributes from one C=C double bond into a new C-C single bond linking neighbouring units.
medium.analogy: A zip joining zipper teeth: no tooth is discarded, the teeth simply interlock through their open ends.
medium.examPointer: Compare with condensation polymerisation when asked: addition polymerisation releases no small molecule, and that contrast is a standard written mark.

check.stem: Which bond in the monomer opens during addition polymerisation?

options.explanation: The double bond's sideways pair is redeployed to link neighbours.
C-H bonds survive intact along the chain.
The sigma pair remains as the backbone bond.
The pi bond must open for chain growth to start.

check.stem: What conditions drive addition polymerisation of ethene?

options.explanation: Industrial poly(ethene) needs both.
UV starts radical substitution, not clean polymerisation.

options.text: An acid catalyst at room pressure
options.explanation: Acid catalysts belong to steam addition.
A catalyst is part of the process.
The chlorine-substituted ethene is the PVC monomer.
Plain ethene gives poly(ethene) with no chlorine.
Propene gives poly(propene) with a methyl side group.
That saturated compound cannot open a pi bond.

check.stem: Why is the atom economy of addition polymerisation always 100 percent?

options.text: Every monomer atom ends up inside the polymer chain
options.explanation: No small molecule departs during addition.
The catalyst is not consumed; economy is about the product.
Elimination would reduce economy - nothing is eliminated here.
Purity is not the atom-economy definition.

check.stem: How does the repeat unit of poly(propene) differ from its monomer propene?

options.text: The double bond becomes a single bond between repeat units
options.explanation: Only the pi bond changes; the methyl side group rides along.
Substituents are conserved on the chain.

options.text: A chlorine replaces the methyl group
options.explanation: No atoms swap identity.
The bonding between units is the difference.

check.stem: Define an addition polymer and name the polymer made from chloroethene.
check.modelAnswer: An addition polymer is the long chain formed when alkene monomers add across their double bonds; chloroethene gives poly(chloroethene), known as PVC.

check.stem: State what the subscript n represents in a drawn repeat unit.
check.modelAnswer: The n counts the enormous number of repeat units that make up the single polymer chain.

check.stem: Explain why addition polymerisation produces no waste products while some other polymerisation routes do.
check.modelAnswer: Addition uses only the pi bond's redistribution to link monomers, so every atom of every monomer is conserved; condensation routes instead expel small molecules such as water when building their links.

check.stem: Poly(propene) is drawn with a repeat unit showing a methyl side group. State the monomer and describe what changed when the chain formed.
check.modelAnswer: The monomer is propene, CH2=CHCH3; on polymerisation its pi bond opened and each former double-bond carbon now bonds through single bonds to neighbouring units, the methyl group riding along unchanged.

lessons.title: Deducing repeat units both ways
lessons.opening: The exam asks the deduction in both directions: draw the repeat unit from the monomer, or recover the monomer from a drawn polymer. One rule powers both - close the double bond to read forward, open the single bond to read backward.
keyPoints: To draw a repeat unit from a monomer, turn the C=C into a C-C single bond and bracket the fragment.
To recover a monomer from a repeat unit, replace the inter-unit single bond with a double bond.
Side groups and halogen substituents carry through unchanged in both directions.
The worked-example drill is identifying monomers from given polymer structures.
Always check the carbon count: repeat unit and monomer share exactly the same atoms.

low.restatement: Forward: monomer's double bond closes to the chain's single bond. Backward: the chain's link reopens into the monomer's double bond. Everything else stays put.
low.analogy: A bridge that is either raised (double bond, separate banks) or lowered (single bond, traffic joins) - the two banks never move.
low.examPointer: Count atoms in your answer against the question's structure - a carbon lost in the redraw is a silent, expensive error.

medium.restatement: The interplay is a bookkeeping identity: monomer C2H3Cl and repeat unit -CH2-CHCl- hold identical atom inventories (2 C, 3 H, 1 Cl), because polymerisation redistributes bonds, never atoms.
medium.analogy: Reading a molecule forward and backward is like transliterating between two scripts - the characters (atoms) are fixed, only the connector (bond order) changes.
medium.examPointer: For substituted monomers, keep the side group on its own carbon exactly as drawn - swapping side groups between carbons is the classic distractor error.

check.stem: What is the repeat unit of poly(chloroethene)?

options.explanation: The chloroethene monomer closes its double bond into the chain link.
That is poly(ethene) - the chlorine went missing.
That doubles the chlorine count.
A repeat unit cannot still carry the double bond.

check.stem: A polymer repeat unit is drawn as -CH2-C(CH3)H- with subscript n. Which monomer produces it?

options.explanation: Reopening the link restores the propene double bond.
Ethene carries no methyl side group.
That monomer holds four carbons; the repeat unit shows two.
No chlorine appears in the unit.

check.stem: Which atom inventory matches both the chloroethene monomer and its repeat unit?

options.explanation: Polymerisation conserves every atom.
A hydrogen vanished - inventories must match.
One carbon dropped in transit.
An extra hydrogen appeared.

check.stem: When drawing a repeat unit, what must stick out through the enclosing brackets?

options.text: The ends of the horizontal single bond
options.explanation: The chain continues through the brackets on both sides.
Side groups stay inside the bracket.
The n sits below-right of the bracket, not through it.
Extension bonds through the brackets are required by the convention.

check.stem: A worked example asks you to identify the monomer of a polymer whose repeat unit carries a phenyl side group. What do you draw?

options.text: The alkene carrying that phenyl group, with its double bond restored
options.explanation: Reopen the single link and keep the side group on its own carbon.

options.text: The polymer chain drawn three times longer
options.explanation: The question wants one monomer, not a longer chain.

options.text: The repeat unit with the phenyl removed
options.explanation: Side groups are conserved - removal invents a different monomer.

options.text: A saturated alkane of the same length
options.explanation: The monomer must carry the double bond.

check.stem: State the single transformation that turns a monomer drawing into its repeat unit.
check.modelAnswer: Replace the monomer's carbon-carbon double bond with a single bond between repeat units, keeping every side group in place, and bracket the fragment with subscript n.

check.stem: State the single transformation that recovers a monomer from a repeat unit.
check.modelAnswer: Replace the inter-unit single bond with a carbon-carbon double bond inside the fragment, giving back the original alkene monomer.

check.stem: Explain why checking the atom inventory catches most repeat-unit errors.
check.modelAnswer: Polymerisation moves no atoms, so monomer and repeat unit must share an identical count of every element - any mismatch exposes a dropped or duplicated group instantly.

check.stem: Poly(chloroethene) incineration aside, deduce the monomer of a polymer whose repeat unit is -CF2-CF2- and state its name.
check.modelAnswer: Reopening the link gives F2C=CF2, tetrafluoroethene, whose polymerisation yields the fluorinated chain; the atom inventory of 2 C and 4 F matches on both sides.

glossary.definition: The small alkene molecule whose repeated addition builds the polymer chain.
The fragment of the polymer chain corresponding to one monomer, drawn in brackets with a subscript n.
The addition polymer of chloroethene, commonly called PVC.

workedExample.prompt: A polymer's repeat unit is drawn as -CH2-CHCl- with subscript n. Identify the monomer and verify the atom inventory.
steps: Reopen the inter-unit single bond into a carbon-carbon double bond.
Keep the chlorine on its own carbon: the fragment becomes CH2=CHCl.
Check the inventory: monomer 2 C, 3 H, 1 Cl equals repeat unit 2 C, 3 H, 1 Cl, so 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 atoms conserved on both sides.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The monomer is chloroethene (vinyl chloride), CH2=CHCl - 6 atoms conserved between monomer and repeat unit.
